 Hydrogen brings cutting-edge intelligence to everyone.

Hydrogen surpasses Argon on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at its default high thinking level (51 vs. 50, and reaching 54 at its highest xhigh thinking setting), while often completing tasks faster than models in its class. signals.title: Building Graph-Enhanced GenAI Applications with graphrag-toolkit - KDnuggets
signals.excerpt:
The graphrag-toolkit is an open-source, Apache 2.0-licensed Python toolkit built by AWS Labs specifically to close that gap. It's made up of two components. The first, and the focus of this article, is lexical-graph, a framework for automatically building a hierarchical knowledge graph from unstructured documents and querying it. The second, BYOKG-RAG (Bring Your Own Knowledge Graph), is a separate approach for teams that already have a knowledge graph and want a multi-strategy question-answering layer over it, without re-extracting anything from scratch.

...

Here's the actual query mechanism, sourced directly from the toolkit's querying documentation. A user's question first gets embedded, and that embedding runs a top-K similarity search against the vector store to find anchor points: statements or chunks that look relevant on the surface. Those anchors then seed one or more graph traversal queries, which pull in thematically connected content from across the graph, not just the chunks that scored highest on similarity alone. The retrieved content, grouped by topic and source, is then supplied to an LLM alongside the original question to generate the actual answer.

One genuinely current fact is easy to miss: the toolkit also ships an older semantic-guided search strategy, but the documentation states directly that it's likely to be retired in a future release. Traversal-based search is both the current default and the one worth building against today, which is exactly the approach used in the hands-on build below.

...

The lexical-graph can expose a tenant's graph as a callable tool through a Model Context Protocol server, letting an agent browse a catalog of domain-specific graphs and pick the right one for a given question automatically. Multi-tenancy lets you host several separate graphs — different document collections, different users — inside the same underlying graph and vector stores rather than provisioning new infrastructure per tenant. Metadata filtering lets you constrain both indexing and querying to specific document subsets based on tags you attach yourself. And versioned updates handle the real-world case this tutorial's one-shot build ignored entirely: re-ingesting a document that's since changed, archiving the old version automatically rather than leaving stale, contradictory information in the graph.

# Releasing MACaQ: one quantizer across modalities

Introducing MACaQ for text, images, audio, video and 3D, with an Apache 2.0 implementation, a paper and an interactive guide.

We are releasing MACaQ, short for Model Agnostic Calibrated Quantization: one quantization recipe for low-precision weights and activations, with examples spanning text, images, audio, video and 3D reconstruction.

The MACaQ implementation is released under the Apache 2.0 license.

## One common building block

Different model architectures share a building block: the linear layer. MACaQ keeps balancing, rotation and quantization decisions local to that layer, avoiding architecture-specific changes to neighboring layers. Calibration and refinement prepare the weights offline; lightweight input transforms are applied during inference.

...

The MACaQ interactive blog brings the method to life through visual and audio comparisons, an explanation of the layer-local design, measured model-size and quality comparisons, and integration workflows for llama.cpp and vLLM. Image and video workflows also use Diffusers.

Read the paper on HF Papers for the full method and experiments, or open the interactive blog to explore the examples.

signals.excerpt:
# DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on Vera Rubin NVL72: 58x Throughput vs. GB300 NVL72 at 387 tokens/s

November 12, 2026 19 min read

Table of Contents

TL;DR: On one NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 rack, vLLM serves DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash at 1.7M tokens/s per GPU while each user gets 387 tokens/s, 58× GB300 NVL72, and reaches 2.52M at peak throughput and 1,810 tokens/s for a single user. The gains come from building on what is new in Rubin: kernels tuned for its split memory and FP4 tensor cores, specialized decode kernels for low latency, and a rack-wide KV cache and Engram tables shared over NVLink.

...

- Rubin-optimized kernels for DEP prefill and decode. 1 We reworked the MoE, attention, GEMM, mHC and indexer kernels for Rubin: bandwidth-bound data stays in each SM's own memory domain, SM107's wider MMA instructions do more work per issue, and kernels start their loads, and their dependents, before they wait. DEP2 prefill steps are about 28% faster, and DEP decode steps about 25% faster.
- A specialized TP decode path for the lowest latency. We perform cross-operator fusions, overlapping computation with communication, and tuning, then spread the model over two trays with TP8, to achieve 1,810 tokens/s (P90) at batch size 1.
- Dynamo workload-aware routing over rack-scale memory pools. Rubin's speed brings much higher concurrency, so we pool the rack's memory: the Mooncake KV pool extends from DRAM to spare HBM, and the Engram tables are sharded across GPU HBM. Even at very high concurrency the prefix hit rate stays at 96.5–97%, and routing alone balances the ranks.

...

We measure performance with the SemiAnalysis AgentX benchmark as a representative agentic serving workload, aligned with our previous posts. Figure 1 compares the two racks' raw throughput (total tokens per GPU per second, including input, cached, and output) and power-normalized throughput, respectively in two tabs.

#### How we measured

We use the same methodology as in our previous GB300 post. For kernels and model forward profiling, `vllm bench forward` times exact prefill and decode batches through the real `execute_model` path, with real weights and real AgentX tokens. We A/B prefill kernels in loops that run for several seconds and report sustained numbers where they differ.

# When One GPU Isn’t Enough: Serving GLM-5.3 Across Two NVIDIA DGX Stations with vLLM

 Nov 13, 2026 

 By Fatima Fall 

 AI-Generated Summary 

- GLM-5.3 NVFP4, a quantized mixture-of-experts model with 753 billion parameters and 40 billion activated per token, requires about 464 GB of GPU memory, exceeding the 252 GB HBM3e on a single GB300 GPU.
- Two NVIDIA DGX Stations connected over ConnectX-8 RDMA serve the model through one OpenAI-compatible endpoint using tensor parallelism (TP=2), with each GPU holding and computing roughly half the weights.
- vLLM launches a distributed service across both Stations, enabling multi-token prediction, FP8 KV-cache storage, and prefix caching to maximize throughput under concurrent load.
- AIPerf benchmarks on the SPEED-Bench Coding dataset show overall output throughput peaking at 607.8 tokens per second at concurrency 16, then falling to 385.0 tokens per second at concurrency 32 with mean request latency of 453.5 seconds.

...

Running a frontier-scale model locally means keeping all its weights in GPU memory; the largest models no longer fit on one machine. Two NVIDIA DGX Stations connected over ConnectX-8 RDMA serve one model through a single endpoint, with tensor parallelism splitting the model weights and computation across both GPUs. 

The NVIDIA GLM-5.3 NVFP4 model, a quantized version of Z.ai’s mixture-of-experts (MoE) model, has 753 billion parameters, with 40 billion activated per token. Sparse activation reduces computation, but all model weights still need to remain available because each token can be routed to different experts. At about 464 GB, the checkpoint exceeds the 252 GB of HBM3e on a single GB300 GPU. This tutorial uses two DGX Stations to keep the weights in GPU memory, with CPU weight offload disabled.

Before starting, connect the two Stations with the Connect Two DGX Stations playbook.

This post shows how to serve GLM-5.3 locally across two NVIDIA DGX Stations with vLLM, send a request, and measure behavior under concurrent load. Tensor parallelism (TP=2) splits the model’s tensors across the two GB300 GPUs. Both Stations compute every request, and Station A returns the answer through one OpenAI-compatible API. By the end, you’ll have a working endpoint and a baseline for how it behaves under load.

...

The script enables multi-token prediction (MTP), a form of speculative decoding: the model’s MTP layer drafts four tokens per step, and vLLM verifies them with the full model before accepting them, so each step can produce several

...

Neither GPU holds a complete copy, and neither can answer a request alone: every token needs both ranks to exchange partial results over the RoCE rail.

...

Table 2, below, shows how throughput and latency change as more requests share the service.

| Configured concurrency | Overall throughput (tok/s) | Mean request latency (s) | Mean TTFT (ms) | Mean inter-token latency (ms/token) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 107.4 | 49.84 | 479.75 | 8.78 |
| 8 | 386.0 | 114.17 | 433.79 | 19.01 |
| 16 | 607.8 | 136.46 | 482.90 | 23.77 |
| 32 | 385.0 | 453.54 | 899.36 | 77.90 |

 Table 2. SPEED-Bench Coding results with prefix caching enabled, four MTP draft tokens per step, and an FP8 KV cache. Latency metrics are means over measured requests; warmup is excluded. TTFT measures time to the first token, which may be reasoning

Overall throughput peaks at 607.8 tok/s at C16. It falls to 385.0 tok/s at C32, where mean request latency is 453.5 s. Higher concurrency also reduces mean per-user throughput, from 115.3 tok/s at C1 to 13.0 tok/s at C32.

...

You now have a 753-billion-parameter model running behind one local API on two NVIDIA DGX Stations, with every weight in GPU memory. That opens up work that’s hard to do on a hosted endpoint: running inference on sensitive or proprietary data, prototyping agents locally, and iterating on prompts without per-token costs.

signals.title: NVIDIA Runs 753-Billion-Parameter GLM-5.3 Across Two DGX Stations | TokenPost
signals.excerpt:
The vLLM setup reached 607.8 tokens per second with 16 requests running at once on the SPEED-Bench Coding dataset.

By Simon Yoon

Published Nov 13, 2026, 1:20 PM EST

...

An NVIDIA demonstration ran the 753-billion-parameter GLM-5.3 NVFP4 model across two connected DGX Stations, showing how local inference can serve a model whose weights exceed one GB300 GPU’s memory.

The model needs about 464 GB of GPU memory for its weights, compared with 252 GB of HBM3e memory on a single GB300 GPU. GLM-5.3 has 753 billion parameters in total and activates 40 billion for each token it generates. The model uses a mixture-of-experts design, so the full set of weights must remain available as tokens are routed to different experts.

NVIDIA linked two GB300 GPUs using ConnectX-8 RDMA and split the model’s tensors and computation between them with tensor parallelism. Station A runs an OpenAI-compatible API endpoint, while Station B works as a worker. Both systems process each request, and Station A returns the completed response.

The deployment used vLLM with prefix caching, an FP8 key-value (KV) cache and multi-token prediction. On the SPEED-Bench Coding dataset, throughput reached 607.8 tokens per second with 16 requests running at once. At 32 concurrent requests, the system delivered 385 tokens per second, and mean request latency was 453.5 seconds. Concurrency refers to the number of requests being handled at the same time.

The setup called for two DGX Stations running Linux and a network connection validated with NVIDIA’s Connect Two DGX Stations playbook. Requirements also included Docker, the NVIDIA Container Toolkit, and access to the dataset and licenses. Each station also required 464 GB of available storage for the model checkpoint, plus space for the vLLM container and temporary files.

signals.title: Introducing OWE-Bench for Long-Horizon Engineering Projects | Mercor Blog
signals.excerpt:
Nov 12, 2026 Research

# Introducing OWE-Bench for Long-Horizon Engineering Projects

Jacob Cole, Cindy Yang, Aravind Selvan, Daniel Babalola, and Bertie Vidgen

Jacob Cole, Cindy Yang, Aravind Selvan, Daniel Babalola, and Bertie Vidgen

Today we're releasing OpenWorldEngineer (OWE-Bench), a frontier coding benchmark of 26 long-horizon engineering and research tasks across software engineering, physical engineering, machine learning, and scientific computing.

We built OWE-Bench to test whether AI agents can make real progress on long-horizon engineering projects, ranging from GPU kernels to aircraft design. Every task is graded on unseen cases and scored on a continuous scale. This means that an agent that speeds up a program halfway to the ceiling earns 50% rather than a pass-or-fail zero.

Claude Fable 5.2 tops the current leaderboard with a score of 54.6%, using an average of 211 million tokens per task attempt. GPT-6 Astra follows with a score of 44.2% using 89 million tokens, and Claude Opus 5.5 at 41.6% using 253 million tokens. No model is close to the benchmark ceiling. Fable 5.2 leads all four domains, with Astra within a few points in physical engineering and scientific computing. The benchmark also successfully differentiates between small and large models, with Inkling and Beam only scoring 1.1% and 3.3% respectively.

...

Tasks for OWE-Bench come in two shapes. In scaffolded tasks, the agent starts from a working codebase and pushes a measurable target such as kernel speed, latency, or error. In end-to-end tasks, it builds the whole artifact from a bare environment: a trained model, a data pipeline, a mechanical design. Depending on the task, agents get 4 to 18 hours per attempt (median 8), for 257 agent-hours across one pass over all tasks, on hardware matched to the task, such as a CPU sandbox, NVIDIA H100 or B300. Seven tasks use a GPU.

 

The 26 tasks span four domains:

- Software engineering (8 tasks): databases, data pipelines, interpreters, and layout, such as exactly-once streaming payments ETL into Iceberg tables with alerts under fault injection
- Physical engineering (5 tasks): CAD reconstruction, structural design, and aircraft, such as a parametric Design/Build/Fly electric aircraft scored over 34 hidden flights spanning three missions
- Machine learning (7 tasks): GPU kernels, training, and inference, such as post-training Qwen3-8B on chess tactics through a metered training service, scored on 1,000 private puzzles
- Scientific computing (6 tasks): chemistry and earth-science modeling, such as relocating an earthquake sequence from supplied seismic observations

...

Evaluation begins with agents submitting an artifact, like a model checkpoint, a data pipeline, a kernel package, a CAD program, or an aircraft design. They are then scored offline by an independent verifier operating without network access, testing the deliverable on CPUs and GPUs using unexposed, held-out inputs. Performance is measured strictly through execution, simulation, or geometric analysis rather than model judgments.

...

Fable 5.2 leads in every domain. It scores 62.2% in software engineering against 49.7% for Claude Opus 5.5 (+12.2pp), and 54.6% in machine learning against 47.8% for Claude Sonnet 5.5 (+6.8pp). The gap with the next best model is far smaller in physical engineering (59.6% vs. 57.3%) and scientific computing (40.2% vs. 39.4%), where GPT-6 Astra is within the margin of error.

signals.title: LlamaIndex vs LangChain: Agent and RAG Orchestration - DEV Community
signals.excerpt:
LlamaIndex vs LangChain: Agent and RAG Orchestration - DEV Community
ke yi
Posted on Nov 11 • Originally published at fp8.co
# LlamaIndex vs LangChain: Agent and RAG Orchestration
# LlamaIndex vs LangChain: Which Should You Use for Agent and RAG Orchestration?
**TL;DR: LlamaIndex and LangChain are MIT-licensed Python frameworks for building LLM applications. LlamaIndex is strongest at the data side of RAG: parsing, indexing, retrieval and query engines. LangChain is strongest at agent orchestration: its `create\_agent` runs on LangGraph, which adds built-in checkpoints and human approval. Choose LlamaIndex for retrieval-heavy apps and LangChain for durable, tool-heavy agents.**
This comparison covers the two frameworks as they stand in November 2026: `llama-index` 0.14 with `llama-index-workflows` 2.x, and `langchain` 1.4 with `langgraph` 1.2. For multi-agent frameworks such as CrewAI and AutoGen, see the CrewAI vs LangGraph vs AutoGen comparison.
### Key Takeaways
* LlamaIndex treats **your data** as the centre of the application. Its core abstractions are documents, nodes, indexes, retrievers and query engines, and an agent usually sits on top of them.
* LangChain treats **the agent loop** as the centre. Its core abstraction in version 1.x is `create\_agent`, a model calling tools in a loop, shaped by middleware and executed on the LangGraph runtime.
* For RAG, LlamaIndex ships more retrieval machinery out of the box: node parsers, ingestion pipelines, routers, response synthesizers, rerankers and a `PropertyGraphIndex`. LangChain gives you the building blocks (loaders, splitters, vector stores, retrievers) and expects you to assemble them.
* For agent orchestration, both are event- or graph-driven. LlamaIndex has event-driven **Workflows** with `@step` functions and `AgentWorkflow` handoffs; LangChain has `create\_agent` plus LangGraph's state graphs.
* Durability is the sharpest difference. LangGraph saves state through a checkpointer after every step. LlamaIndex documents that Workflows have **no built-in checkpointer**: you snapshot `Context` yourself or use the DBOS integration.
* The two combine cleanly. A common production pattern is LlamaIndex for ingestion and retrieval, exposed as a tool to a LangChain or LangGraph agent.
## What are LlamaIndex and LangChain?
Both started in late 2022 as Python libraries for connecting large language models to external data and tools. They have since grown in different directions, and that history explains most of the trade-offs below.
**LlamaIndex** (originally GPT Index) is an MIT-licensed framework maintained by LlamaIndex, Inc. It began as a way to index private documents so an LLM could answer questions about them, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is still its centre of gravity. You load data into **Documents**, split them into **Nodes**, build an **Index** (most often a `VectorStoreIndex`), and query it through a **Retriever** or a **Query Engine** that also synthesises the answer. Agents arrived later and are built on **Workflows**, an event-driven orchestration layer now published as its own package, `llama-index-workflows`. The company also sells hosted document services such as **LlamaParse** for parsing complex PDFs, which the open-source framework can call but does not require.
**LangChain** is an MIT-licensed framework from LangChain, Inc. It began as a library of chains and integrations, and with the 1.0 release it was refocused around agents. The main entry point is now `create\_agent` from `langchain.agents`, which the documentation describes as a model calling tools in a loop, wrapped in a harness of prompt, tools and **middleware**. That agent runs on **LangGraph**, the company's lower-level orchestration runtime, so it inherits LangGraph's state, persistence and interrupts. Retrieval is still there (document loaders, text splitters, embeddings, vector stores and retrievers), but it is one capability among many rather than the organising idea.
A short way to remember them: LlamaIndex is a data framework that learned to run agents, and LangChain is an agent framework that also does retrieval.
## How do LlamaIndex and LangChain compare at a glance?
|Dimension|LlamaIndex|LangChain|
|**Centre of the design**|Data: indexes, retrievers, query engines|Agent loop: model, tools, middleware|
|**Current versions (Nov 2026)**|`llama-index` 0.14, `llama-index-workflows` 2.x|`langchain` 1.4, `langgraph` 1.2|
|**RAG primitives**|Documents, Nodes, `IngestionPipeline`, `VectorStoreIndex`, `PropertyGraphIndex`, query engines, response synthesizers|Loaders, text splitters, embeddings, vector stores, retrievers|
|**Agent entry point**|`FunctionAgent`, `ReActAgent`, `CodeActAgent`|`create\_agent`|
|**Orchestration model**|Event-driven Workflows (`@step`, typed events)|LangGraph state graph (nodes, edges, shared state)|
|**Multi-agent**|`AgentWorkflow` with `can\_handoff\_to`, orchestrator agents, custom Workflows|Subagents as tools, LangGraph supervisors and handoffs, Deep Agents|
|**Durable execution**|Snapshot `Context.to\_dict()` yourself, or DBOS integration|Built-in checkpointers (in-memory, SQLite, Postgres)|
|**Human-in-the-loop**|`InputRequiredEvent` / `HumanResponseEvent`|`HumanInTheLoopMiddleware`, LangGraph `interrupt()`|
|**Languages**|Python, TypeScript (LlamaIndex.TS)|Python, JavaScript/TypeScript|
|**Commercial add-ons**|LlamaParse and hosted document services|LangSmith tracing, evaluation and deployment|
|**License**|MIT|MIT|
|**Best fit**|Document-heavy RAG and knowledge assistants|Tool-heavy agents with approvals and long-running state|
## Which is better for RAG: LlamaIndex or LangChain?
For a retrieval-heavy application, LlamaIndex usually gets you further with less code, because more of the RAG pipeline is a named, configurable component instead of something you write.
**LlamaIndex's RAG stack is layered.** An `IngestionPipeline` runs a list of transformations (node parsers, metadata extractors, embedding models) over your documents and can cache results so re-ingesting a changed corpus only processes what changed. Indexes then decide how those nodes are stored and looked up. On the query side, a query engine combines a retriever, optional node postprocessors (similarity cut-offs, rerankers) and a response synthesizer with selectable response modes. A `RouterQueryEngine` picks between several query engines based on their descriptions, and a `PropertyGraphIndex` builds and queries a knowledge graph when vector similarity alone misses relationships. Each of these is replaceable without rewriting the others.
The minimum version is four lines:
```
from llama_index.core import SimpleDirectoryReader, VectorStoreIndex

...

```
**LangChain's RAG stack is a kit of parts.** You choose a loader, split with something like `RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter`, embed into one of many vector store integrations, and get a retriever from the store. signals.title: Together AI Unveils FOSCAR to Accelerate LLM Inference on NVIDIA GPUs | Tech Pulse | TheNextGenTechInsider
signals.excerpt:
# Together AI Unveils FOSCAR to Accelerate LLM Inference on NVIDIA GPUs

Researchers have introduced FOSCAR, a kernel library that utilizes affine folding to optimize 2-bit and 4-bit KV cache decoding. The tool provides significant speedups for LLM inference on NVIDIA H100 and B200 architectures.

Hiren Dave

Founder

Nov 11, 2026• 3 min read

...

Affine folding produces the same attention output as full dequantization while reducing scale-and-offset operations by up to two orders of magnitude source.

...

## FOSCAR: Accelerating LLM Decode Attention via Affine Folding

Researchers from Together AI and the University of Sydney have introduced FOSCAR, a kernel library designed to optimize 2-bit and 4-bit key-s-value (KV) cache decoding for large language model (LLM) inference, according to their research paper.

The development addresses a critical bottleneck in low-bit quantization: while compressing the KV cache reduces high-bandwidth memory (HBM) traffic, the instruction-issue throughput required to dequantize each element—specifically applying scale and offset—often limits latency gains. On H100 GPUs, existing fused kernels have been shown to reach less than 31% of peak HBM throughput due to this arithmetic overhead source.

...

FOSCAR utilizes a technique called affine folding to bypass per-element dequantization. Instead of applying scale and offset to every individual value, the kernel applies these transformations to the partial matrix products or the query/value operands.

Key technical specifications include:

- Mathematical Equivalence: Affine folding produces the same attention output as full dequantization while reducing scale-and-offset operations by up to two orders of magnitude source.
- Hardware Optimization: The library features warp-specialized pipelines specifically tuned for NVIDIA Hopper (H100) and Blackwell (B200) architectures, utilizing `wgmma` and `tcgen05` instructions.
- Instruction Efficiency: Optimized bit manipulation allows for direct feeding of KV operands to Tensor Cores, requiring only 1 and 0.19 ALU instructions per element for INT2 on H100 and B200, respectively source.

## Performance Results

Benchmarks demonstrate substantial speedups across modern NVIDIA architectures:

- NVIDIA H100: FOSCAR INT2 and INT4 kernels achieved geometric-mean speedups of $3.36\times$ and $2.83\times$ over the FlashInfer BF16 baseline source.
- NVIDIA B200: The kernels achieved speedups of $2.67\times$ (INT2) and $2.30\times$ (INT4) over FlashInfer BF16 source.
- Serving Throughput: When integrated into the SGLang engine, FOSCAR increased peak aggregate throughput on long-context workloads by up to $170\%$ compared to 2-bit baselines and $341\%$ compared to 16-bit baselines source.

## Availability

The FOSCAR kernel library is open-source and available via GitHub.

signals.title: An Agent That Searches, Outlines, and Reads Entire Documents Outperforms Chunk-and-Embed Retrieval
signals.excerpt:
Published Nov 13, 2026

Retrieving documents chunk by chunk works well with many types of text, but it can fail with documents in which the meaning of a given span — say, numbers in a table — depends on particulars found elsewhere on the page — say, the label of their units. Researchers assigned agents to keep all the necessary information in view. 

What’s new: Sagar Tamang, Ayush Vyas, and Tabarakul Hazarika at Indian Institute of Technology Patna and TwoSpoon, an independent tech lab, developed Reliable Embedding-free Agentic Document-search (READ). Their method replaces vector-based retrieval with an agentic harness and specialized search tools. 

Key insight: For RAG-style retrieval, a document is divided into chunks that are embedded, and a model retrieves chunks whose embeddings are similar to the embedding of the query. But this approach can fail with documents such as financial or scientific reports, where numbers in a table gain important meaning from units or dates that may lie many lines away, or legal briefs, in which words may have special meanings that are defined many paragraphs away. An agent with tools to navigate undivided documents can look beyond predefined chunks.

How it works: The authors used the READ method with Gemini 2.5 Pro.

- The system had access to three tools: (i) A keyword-search tool returned matching line numbers, (ii) an outline tool listed section headings with line numbers, and (iii) a text-reader tool fetched specific line ranges.
- Given a query like, “What is the mathematical difference between the Fiscal Deficit and the Revenue Surplus for the year 2024-2025?,” the READ agent activated a loop that generated a search term such as “Fiscal Deficit,” scanned a document for the term, checked matching line(s) against the document outline, and read the text from the table headers to the matching line(s).
- Within the loop, the model refined its query when it got too many hits, too few hits, or insufficient information to make sense of what it found. Each refinement repeated the loop with a new search term or a new range to be read.

Results: The authors used READ, RAG-style retrieval, and RAG-style retrieval in an agentic loop to answer 51 questions about a 780-page financial report published by the government of Gujarat, India. All systems were based on Gemini 2.5 Pro. READ answered 58.8 percent of the questions correctly, outperforming both RAG-style retrieval (15.7 percent) and RAG-style retrieval in an agentic loop (27.5 percent)

signals.title: AMD Quark quantizes Qwen3.8-Flash-Next to UINT4 for 128 GB Ryzen AI Halo edge deployment
signals.excerpt:
# AMD Quark quantizes Qwen3.8-Flash-Next to UINT4 for 128 GB Ryzen AI Halo edge deployment

Brief written by the FOSSWire AI editor from AMD ROCm · How we write

 November 12, 2026 · 2 min read 

AMD's Quark quantization toolkit enables Qwen3.8-Flash-Next to run on Ryzen AI Halo's unified memory by compressing expert weights to UINT4 and replacing the 51 GB FP8 n-gram table with a 1.3 GB calibrated per-token lookup, cutting checkpoint storage from ~130 GB to ~80 GB.

## Summary

AMD has published a technical evaluation demonstrating how its Quark quantization framework can fit the Qwen3.8-Flash-Next large language model onto consumer-grade Ryzen AI Halo hardware with 128 GB of unified memory. The approach combines activation-aware weight quantization (AWQ) to compress routed expert weights to 4-bit unsigned integers (UINT4) with a novel replacement for the model's massive n-gram lookup table. Rather than loading the ~51 GB FP8 n-gram table, AMD tested a calibrated per-token table of only ~1.3 GB that supplies token-specific vectors without local context dependency, plus a zero-lookup baseline for comparison.

The evaluation measures accuracy tradeoffs across thinking and non-thinking modes on benchmarks including MMLU-Pro, coding tasks, and parallel tool-calling. Results show that several thinking-mode scores remain stable even without the full n-gram table, while the calibrated per-token table recovers most of the accuracy loss from zero lookup on non-thinking benchmarks. This work addresses a concrete deployment constraint: unified memory architectures like Ryzen AI Halo cannot offload the n-gram table to separate CPU memory without consuming the same shared pool, making table compression essential for leaving room for the KV cache and runtime buffers.

## Quantization strategy and n-gram table compression

- UINT4 AWQ expert quantization: AMD Quark applies activation-aware weight quantization with group size 128 to the model's routed expert weights, reducing precision from BF16 to 4-bit unsigned integers as the foundation for edge deployment.
- N-gram table architecture: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next uses bigram and trigram hashing at Layer 2 to retrieve learned vectors from a context-dependent table, distinct from ordinary token embeddings; this table contributes ~102 GB in BF16 or ~51 GB in FP8 to checkpoint storage.
- Calibrated per-token replacement (U): A ~1.3 GB table providing one fixed vector per token ID, independent of preceding context, replaces the full n-gram lookup; ordinary token embeddings, output head, and downstream layers remain unmodified.
- Memory-constrained deployment target: Ryzen AI Halo's unified memory architecture means CPU/GPU memory is not separable; the ~130 GB FP8-table checkpoint leaves insufficient headroom for OS, KV cache, and runtime buffers on 128 GB systems.
- Accuracy evaluation scope: Tests cover xhigh reasoning-effort thinking mode, MMLU-Pro, coding benchmarks, and parallel tool-calling with response-length analysis; the calibrated U table recovers most non-thinking accuracy loss versus zero lookup while maintaining several thinking-mode scores.

...

This demonstration shows that open-weight models approaching frontier scale can be adapted for local inference on consumer hardware with unified memory, reducing reliance on cloud APIs for privacy-sensitive or latency-critical applications. For the ROCm and Ryzen AI ecosystem, Quark's quantization pipeline provides a reproducible path to deploy large mixture-of-experts models on AMD consumer silicon, though independent verification of the accuracy tradeoffs and replication of the calibration methodology outside AMD's controlled evaluation remains to be seen.

signals.title: Introducing Loom: agent memory that keeps up with your code
signals.excerpt:
Shared agent memory, checked against your code as it changes.

Loom is an open-source tool built on ClickHouse. It gives coding agents a shared code index and a place to keep what they learn, so the next session doesn't start from zero.

...

Loom keeps memory and a code index in the same ClickHouse database, under one set of permissions. A maintainer's note gets stored with its source and linked to the code it describes, so you can tell later whether it's still accurate. Every run gets logged too: what the agent loaded, what it cost, and whether it actually finished.

It's open-source, and any team can run it against its own repository, with its own agents.

Memory and the code index work fine on their own, but they're built to work together! A client connects over MCP, the HTTP API, or the Python and TypeScript SDKs, and that one connection can save memories, search code, record runs, and search documents.

...

When an agent asks memory a question, Loom doesn't run one nearest-neighbour lookup. It embeds the question and runs several searches in ClickHouse at once: a vector search over the fact embeddings, a keyword search with BM25 scoring over the same facts, a pass over verbatim chunks of long values, and, when the question names people or services, a hop through the entity graph. Every one of those is scoped to the namespaces the caller can read inside the query itself, not filtered afterwards.

signals.title: Huawei Open-Sources MACaQ, Quantizes 122B Model in 64 Minutes | AI Weekly
signals.excerpt:
By Alexis Dufresne · Published November 12, 2026 at 09:29 UTC · Updated November 13, 2026 at 09:47 UTC 

## TL;DR

- The arXiv paper was submitted November 7 and revised November 11, confirming peer review preceded the GitHub open-source release by days.
- MACaQ streams one linear layer at a time, keeping peak GPU RAM at 32.5GB for a 122B model by design, not by hardware-specific tricks.
- vLLM users gain 2.58x throughput immediately; llama.cpp users receive no activation speedup yet, as that integration remains incomplete.

Huawei's Cloud & AI lab says it can quantize a 122B-parameter model in 64 minutes using 32.5 GB of device memory. The claim opens the README of MACaQ, a new Apache 2.0 quantization framework the group published on GitHub under the huawei-csl handle.

MACaQ stands for Model Agnostic Calibrated Quantization, and the stated reach is wide for one release. It targets llama.cpp with 2/3/4-bit GGUF outputs for text, vLLM with W4A4 or weight-only serving, Diffusers with W4A4 for image, video and audio generation, and PyTorch with W4A4 for speech. The repo lists Ascend CANN kernel work shipping via pull requests. Supported models named in the README include Qwen3 variants at 4B, 27B, 30B, 35B and 80B, OLMoE-1B-7B, FLUX.2-klein-4B, Wan2.2-TI2V and Stable Audio 1.0. The project's tagline reads "High-quality GGUF for local inference. Model-agnostic quantization beyond text."

On accuracy, the authors are blunt. They claim MACaQ reaches "lower perplexity than MR-GPTQ and DuQuant++, or match their best Llama-3-8B perplexity with 11× less quantization time." For Qwen3.8-27B under W4A4, the project reports 2.33x prefill and 2.58x decode speedups against a BF16 baseline, with perplexity shifting from 2.8463 to 2.8994. A pre-quantized Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-MACaQ-R GGUF ships alongside the code.

...

Huawei's simultaneous arXiv paper, Apache 2.0 code, and pre-quantized GGUFs signal a coordinated research-to-deployment push timed to build open-source credibility while US sanctions constrain hardware access. Confirmed 2.58x vLLM throughput gains put GPTQ-family maintainers on defense, but an incomplete llama.cpp integration leaves a large share of the local-inference community unreached for now.
